sections.heading: Key Features and Benefits
sections.body:
Four burners in one row. One cook can run four pots side by side without reaching over hot pans, so service is faster and safer.

Strong mild steel frame. Welded mild steel carries heavy sufurias day after day, and it is easy to repair, so the stove keeps working for years at a low cost.

Low working height. Medium and large pots stay at a comfortable stirring level, which reduces strain and spills during long cooking shifts.

Lower support rail. The legs are tied together, so the stove stays rigid and steady even with all four burners loaded.

sections.heading: Who It Suits and Where It Is Used
sections.body:
It suits hotels and restaurants that cook several dishes at once, school and college kitchens, hospital kitchens, catering companies and outdoor event cooking.

Many kitchens use a long mild steel stove like this as the main cooking line, with a separate fryer or griddle beside it.

sections.heading: Getting the Most from a Four Burner Line
sections.body:
Arrange the burners by task. Many cooks keep the two outer burners for big pots of rice and stew that cook for a long time, and use the middle burners for quick jobs such as frying onions, warming sauces or boiling tea. This keeps the busiest pots within easy reach and stops staff reaching across open flames.

Use lids wherever you can. A covered pot boils sooner and uses less gas, which adds up over a long day of service.

sections.heading: Mild Steel or Stainless Steel?
sections.body:
A mild steel frame costs less than stainless steel and is very strong, but it needs to be kept dry and repainted from time to time to prevent rust. Stainless steel resists rust and is easier to wipe clean, at a higher price.

If your kitchen is very wet or you need a showroom finish, compare this stove with our stainless steel ranges. For heavy, everyday bulk cooking on a budget, mild steel is a practical choice.

sections.heading: What to Check Before Buying
sections.body:
Measure the space along your wall or cooking area, leaving room on both ends to work safely. Check that your gas regulator, hose and cylinder bank can supply four burners running together.

Install the stove under a hood or in a well ventilated area, on a level, non-flammable floor.

sections.heading: Care and Maintenance
sections.body:
Clean spills off the burners and frame once the stove has cooled, and keep burner ports clear so the flame stays even. Touch up chipped paint on the mild steel to stop rust spreading.

Check gas hoses and connections regularly with soapy water and replace any part that leaks or cracks.

h1: 4 Ring Mild Steel Gas Burner for Bulk Cooking
short_description: When you cook in bulk, a powerful burner saves both time and gas. This 4 ring mild steel gas burner gives you four controllable flame rings under one large pot, on a low and heavy stand that keeps big sufurias steady. It is the burner of choice for schools, hotels and caterers across Kenya.

sections.heading: Key Features and Benefits
sections.body:
Four flame rings with brass valves. Light just the centre ring to simmer or keep food warm, then open the outer rings for a fast boil. You use only the gas you need.

Wide, even flame. Heat spreads across the whole base of a large pot, so bulk dishes cook evenly and you wait less for water to boil.

Low mild steel stand with a grid top. A heavy, full pot sits securely, and tall pots stay at a safe working height for stirring and lifting.

Built to last. The welded mild steel frame handles daily heavy use and is easy to maintain.

sections.heading: Who It Suits and Where It Is Used
sections.body:
This burner is popular in school and college kitchens, hospitals, prisons and other institutions, hotels preparing large batches, catering companies and community events.

It is also a smart addition next to a standard cooker, taking the heaviest pot off the main range.

Because the stand is compact and open, it is easy to carry to an outdoor cooking area for weddings, harambees and church functions, then bring back to the store afterwards.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes to Avoid
sections.body:
Do not run all four rings under a small pot. The flame will lick up the sides, waste gas and overheat the handles. Match the number of rings to the size of the pot.

Avoid placing the burner on soft ground or uneven tiles. A full big pot is heavy, and the stand must sit level so the pot cannot slide.

Never leave a lit burner unattended, and keep the gas cylinder upright, away from the flame and out of walkways.

sections.heading: Using Fuel Wisely
sections.body:
Because each ring is separate, you only burn the gas you need. Use all four rings to bring a pot to the boil, then close the outer rings and simmer on one or two. Over a full day of institutional cooking, this habit saves a noticeable amount of gas.

A well-fitted lid on the pot also cuts cooking time and fuel use.

sections.heading: What to Check Before Buying
sections.body: Confirm your gas supply, regulator and hose can feed a multi-ring burner. Measure your biggest pot so it sits fully on the stand. Place the burner on a level, non-flammable surface with good ventilation.

sections.heading: Care and Maintenance
sections.body:
Brush food and soot off the rings once cool, and keep every port open for an even flame. Keep the mild steel stand dry and touch up the paint where it chips.

Check hoses and valves often with soapy water, and close every valve and the cylinder after use.

sections.heading: What to Check Before Buying
